plan.contextChunk: This figure shows one undirected weighted graph in which a spanning tree has been picked out by shading. Nine circular vertices carry italic letters: b, c, and d sit across the top, e at the right, f at the lower right, g along the bottom, h at the lower left, a at the left, and i in the middle. Fourteen straight edges join them, each annotated with an integer weight: a-b is 4, b-c is 8, c-d is 7, d-e is 9, a-h is 8, b-h is 11, h-i is 7, h-g is 1, g-i is 6, i-c is 2, c-f is 4, g-f is 2, d-f is 14, and e-f is 10. Eight of those edges, namely a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e, c-i, c-f, h-g, and g-f, are drawn with a broad gray band running behind the line, while the other six remain thin black strokes. The shading is what the reader compares against: it marks an acyclic subset that still reaches every vertex, so the weights along it can be summed and weighed against the heavier unshaded edges it leaves out. The drawing supplies a concrete instance of the wiring problem, in which pins are vertices, possible interconnections are edges, and an edge weight is the amount of wire needed to make that connection.

demo_steps.title: The wiring problem
demo_steps.narration: Nine pins must be connected; every possible interconnection is an edge and its weight is the length of wire it would need. All fourteen candidate connections are shown, none chosen yet.

demo_steps.title: Cheapest links first
demo_steps.narration: Adding edges one at a time, the light connections h–g (1), g–f (2) and c–i (2) appear. Watch the reached-vertex markers spread outward — the set stays acyclic the whole time.

demo_steps.title: Spanning every vertex
demo_steps.narration: By the eighth edge all nine vertices are reached with exactly 8 = 9 − 1 edges and no cycle. The running total is 37 — the minimum possible wire length.

demo_steps.title: Compare the edges left out
demo_steps.narration: Click the heavy unshaded edges such as d–f (14) and b–h (11): each would close a cycle and cost more than an edge already in the tree, so it is excluded.

demo_steps.title: A minimum spanning tree is not unique
demo_steps.narration: Swap b–c (8) for a–h (8): the gray band shifts, the tree still spans all nine vertices with no cycle, and the total weight is still 37.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A minimum spanning tree is defined by its total weight, not by its shape — swapping b–c for the equally heavy a–h gives a different tree that is just as minimal at 37.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape layout, roughly the classic CLRS arrangement: a at far left mid-height; b upper-left; c top-center; d upper-right; e far right mid-height; f lower-right; g bottom-center; h bottom-left; i center, slightly above g. Vertices are light-gray filled circles with black outlines and italic serif letters. Edges are straight black lines; tree edges get a thick pale-gray band (about four times the line width) drawn behind the black stroke so the black line still shows. Weight numerals in large serif type sit just off each edge, outside the polygon where possible (8 above b–c, 7 above c–d, 4 left of a–b, 9 upper-right of d–e, 11 beside b–h, 8 lower-left of a–h, 7 beside h–i, 6 beside g–i, 2 right of i–c, 4 right of c–f, 14 beside d–f, 10 lower-right of e–f, 1 below h–g, 2 below g–f). Keep a small total-weight readout and a status line for the selected edge in a corner, visually separate from the graph.

authoredContext: We can model this wiring problem with a connected, undirected graph G D .V; E/, where V is the set of pins, E is the set of possible interconnections between pairs of pins, and for each edge .u; _x0017_/ 2 E, we have a weight w.u; _x0017_/ specifying the cost (amount of wire needed) to connect u and _x0017_. We then wish to find an acyclic subset T _x0012_ E that connects all of the vertices and whose total weight w.T / D X .u;_x0017_/2T w.u; _x0017_/ is minimized. Since T is acyclic and connects all of the vertices, it must form a tree, which we call a spanning tree since it “spans” the graph G. We call the problem of determining the tree T the minimum-spanning-tree problem. 1 Figure 23.1 shows an example of a connected graph and a minimum spanning tree.

discrepancies: The generated figure adds an in-canvas legend/readout strip along the bottom ('tree edge / excluded edge / Tree weight: 37 / Selected: —') that does not exist in the source; it changes the default composition from a pure graph drawing to a graph + chart chrome.

Stroke weights and node scale are lighter than the source: the source draws very heavy black edges, large bold-outlined vertex circles and very large numerals, whereas the rendered version reads as a thinner, smaller-scale diagram at inline width.

The source renders the highlighted tree edges as a gray band flanked by two black rules (a double-line look); the generated version draws a single black line centered on the gray band, so the highlight reads slightly differently.
Edge-weight numerals are noticeably smaller relative to the vertex letters than in the source, where weights and vertex labels are of comparable, very large size.

Render tree highlights as a gray band with two thin black rules along its edges (as in the source) rather than a single centered black line.
